For procurement teams · Uganda

National content and procurement in Uganda: notes for buyers

In Uganda’s oil and gas sector, land surveying, environmental studies and IT services are reserved for Ugandan companies, registered entities and citizens, and suppliers to the crude export pipeline must generally be on PAU’s National Supplier Database. Many public tenders are reserved for national or long-established resident providers. These notes set out the rules and what they mean for a mapping or drone survey contract. A summary of public rules as of 27 September 2026, for orientation; it is not legal advice.

Send tender documents How we work

In short

Four questions every supplier file should answer

Reserved services

Does the scope fall within a service the petroleum national content regulations reserve, such as land surveying or environment studies, and does the supplier qualify to deliver it?

Registrations

Does the contract need listing on PAU’s National Supplier Database, e-GP registration or a PPDA reservation category, and which does the delivering party have?

Drone approvals

If the scope includes drone work, who owns and registers the drones, and which UCAA approvals and CDF clearance will be in place for this job?

Data

Where will imagery and results be processed and stored, and on what basis under the Data Protection and Privacy Act for any transfer out of Uganda?

Oil and gas

The petroleum national content regulations

Midstream Upstream
Instrument Petroleum (RCTMS) (National Content) Regulations 2016, S.I. 34 of 2016 Petroleum (EDP) (National Content) Regulations 2016, S.I. 44 of 2016
The duty “Every licensee, contractor and subcontractor shall reserve contracts for goods and services specified in the Schedule to be provided by Ugandan companies, registered entities and Ugandan citizens” (reg 11) The same duty for licensees, operators, contractors and subcontractors (reg 10)
The Schedule 15 items 16 items
Exceptions With PAU’s approval, where local capacity is lacking (reg 11(4)) No written exception clause
Items that touch mapping work Land surveying; environment studies and impact assessments; communications and information technology services The same three

A “Ugandan company” (reg 4 in both) is incorporated under the Companies Act 2012, “provides value addition to Uganda”, “uses available local raw materials”, “employs at least 70% Ugandans” and is approved by PAU. A registered entity is a Ugandan-owned business name or partnership.

Bidding. In the midstream regulations, national content is a qualification requirement, upcoming contracts are advertised in at least two national newspapers at least a month ahead, and contract terms are capped (reg 12).

The crude export pipeline

The 2021 special-provisions Act (Act 25 of 2021) for the crude export pipeline requires its suppliers to be registered on PAU’s National Supplier Database, with exceptions where goods, works or services “are not available in Uganda” and for time-limited emergency services (s.15). Contracts listed in the project’s national content appendix are reserved for “Ugandan parties”; where capacity is insufficient, PAU may consent to international procurement, preferably through a Ugandan joint venture (s.24). Where goods or services are not available in Uganda, a foreign supplier may deliver through “a Ugandan joint venture with Ugandan parties approved by the Authority and registered on the national supplier database” (s.25).

Registration

PAU’s National Supplier Database

The National Supplier Database (NSD) is PAU’s register of suppliers to the oil and gas sector. Under PAU’s guideline (updated 1 June 2026):

  • registration is online only and open all year;
  • verification takes up to two months;
  • a listing lasts three years, with an annual profile update;
  • a foreign entity’s certificate of incorporation, tax clearance, social-security compliance and shareholding and director information are notarised in its home country and then attested by the relevant mission.

Portals

  • PAU National Supplier Database
  • e-GP Uganda, for public procurement
  • PPDA

Portals were checked on 27 September 2026; some respond slowly.

Public procurement

The PPDA reservation schemes

PPDA Guideline No. 12 of 2024, on reservation schemes to promote the participation of local providers, commenced on 22 March 2024. It covers procurement by central and local government above set values, funded by the Government or by donors, except where a development partner’s funding conditions limit the reservations (§1.3).

  • National providers: Ugandan citizens, and providers registered in Uganda and wholly owned and controlled by Ugandans. Consultancy, non-consultancy and works contracts up to set values are reserved for them.
  • Resident and EAC providers: companies incorporated in Uganda but not national, and providers operating in the East African Community for at least ten years. A further band of contracts is reserved for them, and both must have been registered for at least ten years when they bid (§1.3(iv)).
  • Opening to others: where the reserved group makes no bid, or a market survey finds no national, resident or EAC provider, the process opens to foreign providers (§2.1(iii), §2.2(iii)–(iv)).
  • Subcontracting on large works: foreign bidders on large road and other public works contracts must “sub-contract a minimum of at least 30% of the value of the works to national or resident providers” (§4.1).
  • Local consultants: a reservation for local inputs and “local consultants where available in works contracts including … EPC projects and Turnkey” (§4.2).

The National Local Content Act 2023 was assented to on 23 June 2023. Its bill set out “to impose local content obligations on a person using public money or utilizing Uganda’s natural resources or carrying on an activity requiring a license; to prioritize Ugandan citizens, Ugandan and resident companies in public procurement”. Its final text was not reviewed for these notes; check it with counsel.

Supplier registration for public tenders is on e-GP Uganda. Some utility tenders for wayleave demarcation and survey equipment in 2026 used open domestic bidding.

Drones and data

Two more rules that shape who does what

Drone ownership

Only Ugandan citizens, lawfully resident foreign individuals, Uganda-registered companies and Government may own a drone (reg 8 of S.I. 96 of 2022), every drone must be registered in Uganda (reg 9), and each operation needs UCAA approval, Chief of Defence Forces clearance, a line-ministry letter and a district sign-off. On petroleum projects, the flying partner must also qualify under the national content rules, because land surveying is reserved. See drone law in Uganda.

Personal data

The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 and its 2021 Regulations govern personal data, which imagery of homes and census records can contain. The Personal Data Protection Office runs organisation registration and breach reporting. Processing or storing personal data outside Uganda needs adequate protection in the destination or the data subject’s consent, so agree with any supplier where the work is done and stored.

How we engage

The same analysis, through the structure the rules require

Where Ugandan law reserves the work for Ugandan companies, registered entities or citizens, or a public tender is reserved for national or resident providers, the work is delivered through a Ugandan partner or joint venture that meets the rules, or as a subcontractor to your appointed consultant or contractor. Our analysis, review and reporting stay the same, and so does the register format your teams receive.

For every contract, the proposal sets out the engagement structure and which registrations the delivering party has in place, so your procurement team can check them before award.

What we never claim

We claim no registration, approval or national content status on this site. Drone work is subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, and we are working towards our own Ugandan drone approvals.

For buyers

What to ask any mapping or drone survey supplier in Uganda

  1. National content status

    For petroleum work: whether the delivering party is a Ugandan company, registered entity or approved joint venture, and its NSD listing.

  2. The reserved items

    Which items in the scope fall within the reserved Schedules, such as land surveying or environment studies, and how the supplier’s structure meets the rule for each.

  3. Public procurement category

    For public contracts: whether the supplier is a national, resident or EAC provider under PPDA Guideline 12 of 2024, and its e-GP registration.

  4. Drone approvals

    Who owns and registers the drones, and which UCAA approvals, CDF clearance, line-ministry letter and RDC-signed risk assessment each flight relies on.

  5. A registered surveyor where one is needed

    Where an output must be signed as a survey, who the registered surveyor is. A structure register is not a cadastral survey.

  6. Data handling

    Where imagery and results are processed and stored, the basis for any transfer out of Uganda, who receives the results, and what is blurred.

Frequently asked questions

Does the PPDA reservation scheme apply to donor-funded contracts?

Not always. Guideline 12 of 2024 covers procurement funded by the Government of Uganda and by donors, but it “shall not apply to procurements funded by Development Partners where the conditions of funding limit the application of the reservations” (§1.3). Check the financing agreement and the bidding document for each contract.

Can a foreign company register on PAU's National Supplier Database?

Yes, online. PAU’s guideline asks a foreign entity for its certificate of incorporation, tax clearance, social-security compliance and shareholding and director information, notarised in its home country and then attested by the relevant mission. Verification takes up to two months and a listing lasts three years, with annual profile updates.

Is a Ugandan subsidiary of a foreign firm a "Ugandan company"?

Only if it meets the definition in the petroleum national content regulations. That means being incorporated under the Companies Act 2012, providing value addition to Uganda, using available local raw materials, employing at least 70 % Ugandans, and being approved by PAU.

Can a foreign company own drones in Uganda?

Not in its own name. Regulation 8 of S.I. 96 of 2022 limits drone ownership to Ugandan citizens, lawfully resident foreign individuals, Uganda-registered companies and Government, so a Uganda-registered company qualifies, and every drone must be registered in Uganda. Regulations 85 and 86 allow an application for exemption, but whether UCAA would grant one to a foreign-owned operator is not known. See drone law in Uganda.

What do you need from us to prepare a proposal?

The route or boundary file, the districts it crosses, the widths or zones to report, the date the record must reflect, the deliverables and the deadline. With a tender, send the documents and tell us the portal, the procurement method and any national content or reservation requirement that applies.

Preparing a tender or a supplier file in Uganda?

Send the tender documents and your supplier forms. The proposal answers each requirement, sets out how the engagement is structured for your contract, and states which registrations the delivering party has in place.
